1.note: The psalmist is using an imperative, but he is communicating a polite request to God rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [God, please give your judgments to the king]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [give your just decisions to the king, yes, give your righteousness to the king’s son]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **judgments**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [your ability to judge rightly]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and give your righteousness to the son of the king]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [your righteous character]

The psalmist is using this possessive form to describe a social relationship. **The son of the king** refers to the king’s offspring. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the king’s son]

2.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [righteously]

The psalmist is saying what he wants God to make happen. See the discussion in the introduction to Psalms about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [I want the king to judge your people with righteousness and your poor with justice]

The psalmist is using the adjective **poor** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [your poor people]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **justice**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [justly]

3.q: יִשְׂא֤וּ הָרִ֓ים שָׁ֘ל֥וֹם לָ⁠עָ֑ם וּ֝⁠גְבָע֗וֹת בִּ⁠צְדָקָֽה
3.note: The psalmist is speaking of **the mountains** and **the hills** as if they were living things that could **bring peace** to the people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May the land produce prosperity for the people, from the mountains to the hills, through righteousness]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **peace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [peaceful conditions]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and may the hills bring peace to the people, in righteousness]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [righteously]

4.note: The psalmist is using this possessive form to describe the poor who are among the people. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [those among the people who are poor]

The psalmist is using the adjective **poor** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the poor people of]

The psalmist is using **sons of** as a common expression of the culture to indicate that a person has a certain characteristic. In this case, people have the characteristic of being needy. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [people who are in need]

The psalmist is using the adjective **needy** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [needy people]

The psalmist is using the adjective **oppressor** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the one who oppresses them]

5.note: The pronoun **they** refers to the people. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could state that explicitly. Alternate translation: [May the people fear you]

The psalmist is using the two extremes of **the sun** and **the moon** together to mean all of time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [as long as the sun and moon endure]

Here, **the face of the moon** represents the presence and duration of the moon. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [as long as the moon exists]

The expression **generation of generations** is an idiom that means “for all successive generations,” that is, “forever.” If your readers would not understand this, you could use an equivalent idiom or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [throughout all future generations]

6.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **rain** nourishes **mown grass** and causes it to grow again, so the king’s rule will nourish and refresh his people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point of comparison explicit. Alternate translation: [like rain that falls on mown grass and refreshes it]

The point of this comparison is that just as **showers** drench and soak the earth, so the king’s influence will thoroughly bless his people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point of comparison explicit. Alternate translation: [like showers that drench the earth]

7.note: The psalmist is speaking of **the righteous** as if they were plants that **flourish** and grow. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May the righteous prosper in his days]

The psalmist is using the adjective **righteous** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the righteous person]
The pronoun **his** refers to the king. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could state that explicitly. Alternate translation: [in the king’s days]

Here, **his days** represents the time period of the king’s reign. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [during his reign]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **abundance** and **peace**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [and experience very peaceful life]

8.note: The psalmist is using two extremes of geography, **from sea to sea** and **from the River to the ends of the earth**, together to mean everywhere. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [over the whole earth, from sea to sea and from the River to the farthest lands]

The psalmist is saying how he wants the king to **rule**. See the discussion in the introduction to Psalms about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [I want him to rule from sea to sea and from the River to the ends of the earth]

The psalmist is using this possessive form to describe the farthest places on **the earth**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the farthest places on earth]

9.note: Here, **his face** represents his presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [kneel before him]

The expression **lick the dust** is an idiom that means to be completely defeated and humiliated. If your readers would not understand this, you could use an equivalent idiom or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [be completely defeated]

9.q: לְ֭⁠פָנָי⁠ו יִכְרְע֣וּ צִיִּ֑ים וְ֝⁠אֹיְבָ֗י⁠ו עָפָ֥ר יְלַחֵֽכוּ
9.note: In both instances, the pronoun **his** refers to the king. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could state that explicitly. Alternate translation: [May desert-dwellers kneel to the king’s face, and may the king’s enemies lick the dust]

10.q: מַלְכֵ֬י תַרְשִׁ֣ישׁ וְ֭⁠אִיִּים מִנְחָ֣ה יָשִׁ֑יבוּ מַלְכֵ֥י שְׁבָ֥א וּ֝⁠סְבָ֗א אֶשְׁכָּ֥ר יַקְרִֽיבוּ
10.note: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [May kings from distant lands, from Tarshish to Sheba and Seba, bring tribute and gifts to him]

The psalmist is using this possessive form to describe the kings who rule in **Tarshish**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the kings who rule in Tarshish]

The psalmist is using this possessive form to describe the kings who rule in **Sheba** and **Seba**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the kings who rule in Sheba and Seba]
The word **Seba** is the name of a region.

11.note: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [And may all kings and nations submit to him and serve him]

The word **And** escalates the stated desire from the specific kings mentioned in the previous verse to **all kings** and **all nations**. Use a connector in your language that communicates this escalation. Alternate translation: [Indeed, may all kings bow down to him]

The psalmist says **all kings** and **all nations** as a generalization to emphasize how widespread the king’s dominion will be. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [kings everywhere … nations everywhere]

12.note: The word **For** introduces the reason why the kings and nations of the preceding verses should honor the king. Use a connector in your language that communicates that what follows is a reason. Alternate translation: [May they do this because he delivers]

The psalmist is using the adjective **needy** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the needy person]

The psalmist is using the adjective **poor** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the poor person]
The pronoun **him** refers to the poor person. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could state that explicitly. Alternate translation: [when no helper is available to that poor person]

13.q: יָ֭חֹס עַל־דַּ֣ל וְ⁠אֶבְי֑וֹן וְ⁠נַפְשׁ֖וֹת אֶבְיוֹנִ֣ים יוֹשִֽׁיעַ
13.note: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [May he show compassion to weak and needy people by saving their lives]

The psalmist is using the adjectives **weak** and **needy** as nouns to mean certain kinds of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [weak people and needy people]

14.q: מִ⁠תּ֣וֹךְ וּ֭⁠מֵ⁠חָמָס יִגְאַ֣ל נַפְשָׁ֑⁠ם וְ⁠יֵיקַ֖ר דָּמָ֣⁠ם בְּ⁠עֵינָֽי⁠ו
14.note: In this verse, the pronoun **he** refers to the kings, **their** refers twice to the needy, and the pronoun **his** refers to the king. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could state that explicitly. Alternate translation: [May the king redeem the lives of the needy from oppression and from violence, and may the blood of the needy be precious in the king’s eyes]

The psalmist is using the singular **life** to refer collectively to the lives of multiple people. If your language would not use a singular noun in this way, you could use the plural form. Alternate translation: [their lives]

The words **oppression** and **violence** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two words together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [from every kind of mistreatment]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **oppression** and **violence**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [from those who oppress them and from those who harm them]

Here, **their blood** represents their lives, especially the shedding of blood through violence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [their lives]

The expression **precious in his eyes** is an idiom that means he considers it to be very valuable. If your readers would not understand this, you could use an equivalent idiom or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and may their lives be valuable to him]

15.note: The psalmist is using this possessive form to describe gold that comes from **Sheba**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from the gold that comes from Sheba]
The word **one** refers to people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could state that explicitly. Alternate translation: [may people give to him … may people pray for him]
The pronoun **they** refers to people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could state that explicitly. Alternate translation: [may people bless him]

The psalmist says **continually** and **all of the day** as generalizations to emphasize how frequently people should pray for and bless the king. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [and may one pray for him continuously; may they bless him constantly]

16.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **abundance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [abundant grain]

Here, **the head** of the mountains represents the tops or summits of the mountains. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [on the tops of the mountains]

The point of this comparison is that the fruit of the grain will sway abundantly, just as the trees of **Lebanon** sway in the wind. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point of comparison explicit. Alternate translation: [may its fruit sway like the trees of Lebanon sway]
The pronoun **its** refers to the grain in the land. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could state that explicitly. Alternate translation: [the grain’s fruit]

The point of this comparison is that just as **grass** grows abundantly on **the earth**, so the people will flourish and multiply in the cities. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point of comparison explicit. Alternate translation: [may the people of the city flourish as abundantly as does the grass of the earth]
The pronoun **they** refers to the people. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could state that explicitly. Alternate translation: [may the people flourish from the city]

17.note: Here, **the face of the sun** represents the presence and duration of the sun. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [as long as the sun shines]

The pronoun **they** refers to the nations, and the pronoun **him** refers to the king. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could state that explicitly. Alternate translation: [may the nations be blessed by the king]
If your language does not use this passive form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [may he bless them]

Here, **blessed** means to have good things done for someone. The psalmist is expressing a desire for the king to bring good things to all people. Alternate translation: [may he do good things for them]

The psalmist says **all of the nations** as a generalization to emphasize how widespread the king’s fame will be. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [nations everywhere]

17.q: יְהִ֤י שְׁמ֨⁠וֹ לְֽ⁠עוֹלָ֗ם לִ⁠פְנֵי־שֶׁמֶשׁ֮ ינין שְׁ֫מ֥⁠וֹ
17.note: Here, **his name** represents the king’s reputation and fame. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May his reputation last forever; may his fame continue to the face of the sun]

18.note: The expression **Blessed be** is a passive verbal form. The psalmist is expressing his desire to praise Yahweh. If it would be unnatural to use that form for this purpose, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I bless Yahweh] or [Let us all praise Yahweh]

The psalmist is not using this possessive form to indicate that the Israelites possess or control God. Rather, he is using it to indicate that Yahweh is the God whom Israel worships. Alternate translation: [who is the God whom Israel worships]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [he alone can do]

19.note: Here, **blessed be** expresses praise to God. This is a doxology in which the psalmist declares that God’s glorious name is worthy of praise forever. If your readers would not understand this blessing formula, you could express this in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [may people praise his glorious name forever]

Here, **the name** represents God’s reputation and character. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his glorious reputation]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [his glorious name]

The expression **be filled** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and let his glory fill all of the earth]

The psalmist is repeating the word **Amen** for emphasis as a way of concluding Book 2 of Psalms (42–72). If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [May it certainly be so]

20.note: This possessive form describes a social relationship, for **son of Jesse** identifies David as the offspring of Jesse. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [, Jesse’s son,]
If your language does not use this passive form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [end here]
